utterances.text: How did you get by without being in proper uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had taken my oath in the Yugoslav People's Army, and I wore those insignia until the end of my active duty, until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other Muslim officers also remained when the VRS was created, did they not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know how many?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. In my unit, perhaps eight or nine people stayed on, I mean officers, who were Croats or Bosniaks. I could perhaps list the names, but as early as June, they quit the service following the order issued by General Mladic, and left to Belgrade, to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And non-commissioned officers who were non-Serb also remained in the VRS, did they not, after the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that one of them stayed but he changed his name. He was Muhamed Talic. He changed his name into Marko and stayed with the army. He was my subordinate. He was an optician in a tank workshop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a pilot by the name, I think, Crnalic was his name, a Bosniak who remained in the VRS and actually flew some of those aircraft we were seeing there on the television just a moment ago, and bombed various villages? Are you familiar with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know a single pilot, because the air force had come from Zagreb to Mahovljani near Banja Luka, and did I not communicate with them except with the commander of the air base in Mahovljani but I did not communicate with other officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There were also many conscripts who were non-Serb, who remained within the VRS after the changeover, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the number. True, some stayed but I wouldn't know the number. But I disagree with your qualification, a large number, because that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if you consider that a very large percentage of the JNA on 18th May was Serb anyhow, I'll agree with you, it couldn't have been a very large number. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the ethnic structure, and I'm referring to Banja Luka, there should have been a larger number of the reserve force in the corps units. And it was precisely the corps units which were reluctant to take up such people, such individuals, because they miss trusted them. They were reluctant to issue them with weapons fearing that they might misuse them, and at the same time, those men were also afraid of joining the units, because they feared for their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Looking, then, on the other side of that coin, there were a number of JNA officers who left the JNA and went off and joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number, yes. Definitely. But I was not with the BH Army. I know that there were men who joined, especially in Tuzla, in Sarajevo, Mostar, and so and so forth, but from Banja Luka, nine -- we were nine of us, Bosniak officers, and none of us joined the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're familiar with Halilovic, Alagic, and Efendic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I met them after the war. I did not know them during the war. They were younger than I was and we were not in the same units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My point is, they were former JNA officers, though, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you read their books?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know Jovan Diviljak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jovan Diviljak happened to be a Serb member of the JNA who joined the Bosnian army, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. A decent, honourable man, a true officer, and a good Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So after 18 May, when you continued to serve in the VRS, you followed the orders that were given to you, did you not, like a good soldier?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And of course after 18 May, this army that you were in was no longer a Yugoslav army but the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in that connection, being a Serb army, it would not be unusual or improper or out of line for there to be legitimate concern about the loyalty of non-Serb officers, would it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You, sir, apparently were quite a remarkable officer. You always got excellent efficiency reports and had a good reputation to the point where even in 1992, when things had started happening in the country, you were appointed as the liaison with United Nations forces who were being assigned to that area, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general staff of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give me a name of the actual person who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That would have been at that point in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have the order. I gave it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you served in that position for a period of time, until things got difficult for you in that regard, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean "difficult" for me. At the beginning of April, I was replaced and appointed commander of the logistics base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You had been appointed on this liaison job when?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th or 7th of February. I have a copy of the order, perhaps in my brief case, but the OTP have a copy too. We can find it. Please don't hold me to my word regarding the exact date, but any way, the beginning of February. So I held the position for about a month and a half, no longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told us in your testimony that you got into some disagreement with Mayor Radic over the billeting of the UN officers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a sort of general proposition, through this period of time, and I'm focusing especially on 1992 here, you really had no serious problems serving as a Muslim officer in the VRS, did you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to be referring, Colonel, as we go along, to your various statements to the Prosecution, and you are entitled to have those statements in front of you to refer to them, if you'd like to, and I can ask the Prosecution to give them to you. It might be fair to you so that you can follow what we are talking about, and we don't get into disputes as to what we are talking about. I think that I'll ask that be done?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Tadic transcripts as well or just the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just the statements, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm starting with the 1995 statement that you gave, and I'll work chronologically from there. So if you can be given the 1995 one now, then we can forge on. The statement I'm going to refer to for the next several moments and maybe the rest of today is the one that you made in 1995. And the first reference I will make is page 11 of the English version. You are speaking at that location about General Uzelac, and how, in 1991, he was always out and around at meetings with SDS leaders, and that there were dinner parties almost every night, and that's where all the decisions were made. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph I'm actually referring to begins with, "Uzelac turned over his duties to General Vukovic." I don't know if you can find that or not, but you might want to look at it. And this group that was out at dinner parties almost every night where all the decisions were made actually wanted you to join them, didn't they, to become part of that group?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's what you said in your statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read it, but yes, that's how it was. I haven't found the exact place in the statement but I agree with what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so they were asking you to become a part of these dinner parties where decisions were made, you, a non-Serb officer. And what you did was refuse to do that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I refused, but for the following reason: I was an officer, true I had taken my oath to the Yugoslav People's Army, my oath of allegiance, and at these meetings something else was discussed and being done. I didn't want to be seen in the company of those people in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the points I'm trying to make, sir, is that they weren't trying to shut you out, were they? But trying to bring you in.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was for Yugoslavia but not for the kind of Yugoslavia that was being tailored there and elsewhere in Serbia and other places. And they knew that I was of pro-Yugoslav orientation and I was of such an orientation, and that is why they wanted me to join them, to keep company with them and to be with them, alongside them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I need you to find this next part, just so you can satisfy yourself that I'm quoting correctly. It's about probably three pages back from the one I just did. It's page 7 in the English version. It has to do with the literacy of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, did you find it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text on page 7 here, in my language, in which it says, "Contrary to that, reserve officers," and above that, "all military conscripts from Serbia, Montenegro," et cetera. I don't know which paragraph you're referring to. Please help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to do that right now. The paragraph begins with "the top three reasons for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's how it begins.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And about halfway through that paragraph, you say this: "There was a recent study reported on Belgrade TV that showed that 85 per cent of the Serb population was illiterate or barely literate, elementary school education. The study shows that these type of people can be greatly influenced by the church and the mass media." That's what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that. On the 18th of May, 1992 -- I'm sorry, 1995, I left Banja Luka and went to Belgrade, and I stayed there for 13 days. And in a weekly called Vreme, a professor at the faculty of philosophy in Belgrade wrote, among other things, that 85 per cent of the Serb people have less than a secondary education, and this is a misquotation of what I said. She said 85 per cent of the population have less than a secondary education. And I stand behind that, that copy of the magazine can be found. It was in the issue at the end of May, 1995. And that is what she said. She was a person who had accurate data and who should be trusted. Unfortunately, the same can be said of Bosnia, at least that is my opinion. This applies to other ethnicities as well, and they were easy prey for manipulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Colonel, what you have just told me is that the statement that's contained within the statement you have in front of you is not correct. It's not what you said. You didn't say that 85 per cent were illiterate? Or if you were misquoted, you were mistranslated or something. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that 85 per cent of the Serb population had an education below the level of a secondary education. And that is what I read in the article at the end of May, 1995, and I quoted from that article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And that would have, of course, referred to all of Yugoslavia, and you've just told us that it probably also fairly reflected the educational level of all the other inhabitants of the country?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Slovenia should be excluded in the part of Croatia. As for the rest, unfortunately, I'm afraid that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the other thing that you say there, the last sentence of your statement, says this: "The study shows that these type of people can be greatly influenced by the church and mass media." Now, was that part of the report that you saw or is that some conclusion you have made as a result of the report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my conclusion. Because that is exactly what happened. That people believed their religious officers, in whose interest it was to create the state of a Greater Serbia, which the Academy of Sciences in Belgrade also discussed and there is such information available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, if that kind of influence happened among the Serb population, I think you'd concede that it also happened among non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here for the break, Mr. Ackerman? Is it convenient for you? So we'll have a 15-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, you gave several statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. One statement between 23 September, 1995 and 31 January, 1996. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And another between 10 January and 13 July of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then another on 10 March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yet another one on 22 August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you gave testimony in the Tadic case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that never in any of those statements, or in any of that testimony, did you ever mention Radoslav Brdjanin? Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's correct. I don't have all the statements here, but I think I didn't mention him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, in statements that you gave to investigators of the Prosecution, after Mr. Brdjanin's arrest in 1998, they asked you about Brdjanin, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Brdjanin was arrested in 1999, not 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he's nodding behind you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'm a year younger than I thought I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You gave one, two, three statements to the OTP after Mr. Brdjanin's arrest in 1999, and in none of those statements did you mention Mr. Brdjanin. And my question was: Surely, the investigators must have asked you about him when they took those statements? I mean, it's why they were talking to you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had asked me about Mr. Brdjanin, I would have certainly answered them. So if it's not contained in my statements, they didn't ask me. And the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem a bit bizarre to you that investigators investigating the Brdjanin case would not ask you on three opportunities if you knew anything about Brdjanin? Isn't that bizarre?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is up to the Prosecution, as to what they are going to ask me. It's not up to me, and I don't wish to enter into such details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest, sir, that they in fact asked you every time, and every time you said you knew nothing about him. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I ask on what possible grounds that's based?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just logic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whose logic, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mine, Your Honour, and perhaps several other people's too. Otherwise it just baffles the mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered questions put to me by the Prosecution, and I stand by what I said. There may be errors in the interpretation. Such as the question of the 85 per cent of the Serbian people being illiterate. That was misinterpreted. And I may allow for the possibility that they -- there may be other minor details that were misrepresented through translation. But basically, I stand by what I said in those statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first time, then -- what you're telling us is, the first time that you ever mentioned to anyone from the Prosecution anything about Mr. Brdjanin was last week in your conversations with Ms. Korner? Suddenly last week, you know about him and not just a little bit, but a lot. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of Mr. Brdjanin since the elections in 1990 because I lived in Banja Luka. Throughout my working life time. And after that, Mr. Brdjanin held political positions. Therefore, it would be illogical for me not to know Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question so I'll ask it again. The first time --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That you ever mentioned to anyone from the Prosecution anything about Mr. Brdjanin was last week in your conversations with Ms. Korner? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember each and every sentence of my statement. I mentioned quite a number of people, personalities. My statements are here before the Tribunal. So that is what you're claiming, it's easy to check that, looking through the statements. I really cannot remember whether I mentioned him somewhere or not in these statements earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And please don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Read them and it's not there or would you like to have them supplied to you. So you can read them all this evening and confirm to yourself that Mr. Brdjanin is not mentioned there? It's up to you, and I don't care which choice you make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can just check that and I'll confirm on behalf of the Prosecution, rather than asking the witness to read through the statements. I mean, when I've checked it myself. Because I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We take it that he's never mentioned -- Mr. Brdjanin is not mentioned in any of those statements. That's a correct affirmation, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor last week that the last time you saw Mr. Brdjanin was in 1994, when he spoke to you in the street and asked if there was anything he could do to help. Do you recall telling the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall. Brdjanin was wearing -- Mr. Brdjanin was wearing a camouflage uniform, at the marketplace in Banja Luka. I was on the other side of the road. He came up to me and asked me, "Selak, are you having any problems of any kind?" I said I was not and I went along my way. I didn't stand around any longer with Mr. Brdjanin, talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that he asked you if there was anything he could do to help. Why would he have asked you if there was anything he could do to help you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin probably knew quite a bit about me, just as I knew about him, and it was quite fair on his part to ask me that. However, I didn't want any help, because knowing what he was doing, and being aware of his abilities, or rather his positions, I didn't want his help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you not at the time have a family member who was quite ill?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My wife was seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And don't you think that that's what he was talking about, wondering if he could help you in any regard with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought about it. I didn't have time either. I thanked him and went along my way, and I struggled alone regarding my sick wife, with the assistance of other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware, or were you aware when he spoke to you that day, that during the war he helped a number of Muslim people who were having problems? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd like that to be true but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know that he helped a great deal -- great number of Muslim people to keep the apartments they had in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know that he was in trouble with members of the SDA and acquired the reputation of being the Schindler of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: SDA or SDS?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: SDS. He was called that in a publication or two? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it? Because the question really is not clear to me. Did you mean the SDS or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The SDS. Do you know that he got in trouble with the SDS because he was helping Muslim people, and in fact a couple of publications referred to him as the Schindler of Banja Luka? Are you aware of that? Did you see those reports?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about those derogatory names, but I do know that the end of 1994, he corrected some of his positions, in my view, and there were comments about that in the press or rather among the citizens in town. I do not recollect the details. After all, it was a long time ago, but I did have information that he had corrected his views in relation to the official policies of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you responded to me, "I know nothing about those derogatory names," what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said that he was referred to as, I don't know whom, what name he was given. I hear that word for the first time. But I'm sorry, I do know for sure that in the course of 1992 and 1993, that the citizens of Banja Luka that I had contact with expressed very negative views about Mr. Brdjanin, but I don't know anything about actual derogatory names he was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't consider it derogatory. Do you know who Oskar Schindler was in World War II?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard something else. I thought I heard another word, not this name that you have just used. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oskar Schindler was a German who saved a number of Jewish people, and that was the reference to Mr. Brdjanin being the Banja Luka Schindler.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jews, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see your answer. Thank you. All right. I'm going to go to your second statement. It's made in the year 2000, and it's page 10 of the English version, January and July of 2000. And if you can find a page, sir, where you begin talking about documents that were shown to you, there is a sentence that begins, "I have been shown some other documents, mainly regular combat reports, and I want to make the following comments." It's on page 10 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Document number 1 is -- is that the one? Or rather, when I list them, starting with number 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll get back to that in a moment. I now want you to at the same time look at the Exhibit DB120. Now, you have before you, sir, a document dated 11 April, 1992, and -- a document authored and signed by Mesud Hasotic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasotic, Colonel Mesud Hasotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this document was written in his capacity as the assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs of --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as we discussed yesterday, Colonel Hasotic was a Bosniak, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to just take you through parts of what he wrote here. At the time this was written, the -- you were still the JNA. You had not converted to the VRS yet, had you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's correct, isn't it, that the official policy of the JNA was to keep Yugoslavia together and oppose the ethnic break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you described this document in your statement, the statement that you have in front of you, from 2000, and it's now paragraph 2 of that page that I referred you to. You described this document --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You described this document there as a document which -- "The attitude reflected in this document" -- no. "This document conveys the official position of the corps command to all its members," correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You also described it as -- said this: "The content of this document clearly reflects the attitudes and the position of the military leadership," correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of the corps command, sir; not of the JNA but the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the words you used were "military leadership," wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he's speaking on behalf of the 5th Corps command. I did not see eye to eye with Colonel Hasotic, and this was one of the reasons for that, and I said so in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's look at the exhibit now, his actual -- what he actually wrote. Beginning at the beginning: "In several crisis areas in BH, there is an escalation of open conflicts of ever-increasing intensity, with tragic consequences in terms of human life and property. The situation is most critical in Kupres, Bijeljina, Bosanski Brod, Sarajevo and Foca. According to some of the evidence received up to 9 April, several hundred people have been killed there, mostly women and children. The most serious suffering is being experienced by the people of Kupres, where heavy fighting is taking place between the armed formations of Croatia and the Serbian people from these parts. The objective of the Croatian state's diabolical plans is to take Kupres, regardless of casualties, and to join up the BH HDZ paramilitaries along the Bugonja-Doboj-Bosanski Brod axis. This would effectively sever the Serbian Krajinas from the remainder of Yugoslavia." Now, that is exactly what happened, isn't it? That area was captured by the Croatian forces and it severed the Krajina from the remainder of Yugoslavia. That's the corridor we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting around Kupres started in late 1994, and it is true that the Croatian forces wanted to take Kupres and that area and to join it to the Republic of Croatia. That was their objective, and we knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report of April of 1992, and I'm talking about -- and let me read the last sentence to you again.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The objective of the Croatian state's diabolical plans is to take Kupres, regardless of casualties, and it's the second part of this that I'm interested in, "To join up the BH, HDZ paramilitaries, along the Bugojno, Doboj, Bosanski Brod axis. This would effectively sever the Serbian Krajinas from the remainder of Yugoslavia." And that is what happened, isn't it? That area was captured by Croatian forces and the Krajinas were separated from Yugoslavia, and that's why there was a later war to open up the corridor. That's all true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the diabolical Milosevic-Tudjman plan, how to break up Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so within that context, yes, it fully tallies with that plan, they would have been separated. They would be separated, but that was the breaking up of Bosnia-Herzegovina by other states, by the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it your answer is that that's true, that that is exactly what happened? What Colonel Hasotic predicted was going to happen happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that objective was not achieved because the Croatian forces never entered Bugojno, Doboj, or Bosanski Brod. That did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How about this? Second paragraph: "Crime, looting and inter-ethnic reprisals have spread over a large part of BH territory. Complete anarchy reigns throughout the republic, and in some communities there is total chaos. The division of the BH MUP into the MUP of the Serbian people's republic and Republic of BH MUP has further threatened the safety of people in multi-ethnic communities." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a sentence down, the very end of that paragraph. It says, "For a long time, RTSA, Sarajevo Radio and TV, showed exhaustive footage of the withdrawal of the army from Macedonia, the intentions behind this are quite clear, namely prepare the people to give the JNA the same type of farewell, read as a fair one, from the republic on that fine day when the Bosnia's turn comes." Now, what he's speaking of there is when the JNA was withdrawn from Macedonia and the pictures of that withdrawal, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that footage about the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia. What I do know, however, is that the Republic of Macedonia wanted and succeeded in keeping all the materiel of the former JNA, and we, from Banja Luka, from the logistics base there, sent columns of vehicles to Macedonia to pull out the materiel that was necessary for the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he's predicting a time, is he not, when the JNA would be withdrawing from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA never pulled out from Bosnia, and the units which had arrived from Croatia, even stayed in Bosnia and even at the Uzice corps, the Novi Sad corps came from Serbia to Bosnia in pursuits of their objectives, that is the official policy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There actually were units of the JNA that left Bosnia, weren't there? Not easily but they did.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The units did not pull out, did not leave. It was soldiers who were serving their military duty in the units of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, until the 18th of May, 1992, left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina but the officers who were Serbs originally from Serbia and Montenegro did not leave the JNA units. They kept their duties and were on the payroll in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, like all the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But wasn't there a unit around mid-May of 1992, that was stationed in Sarajevo, maybe at a military academy there, that attempted to leave Sarajevo and return to Belgrade in accordance with the order that the JNA should return to Serbia? Don't you recall that incident, when that unit tried to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the high military academy centre in the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo, there were some small units providing security, be it physical or logistical, and a goodish number of people in those units wanted to leave, and, yes, that was a problem. But I'm not aware -- I was not familiar with the details of that whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Did it not, where those soldiers, those JNA soldiers were actually attacked by Muslim forces or paramilitaries in Sarajevo? That happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not living in Sarajevo at the time, and I'd rather not say something wrongly. I really do not have the accurate information, and I'd rather not speak about it. I simply do not know. Yes, there was an incident but I'm not aware of any of its details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this present series of questions, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has to do with the changing of the guard, so to speak, between the JNA and the VRS and all the difficulties that surrounded that and the essential truth of this document by Colonel Hasotic, which I will finally get around to asking the last question about. It all is building up to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, the last sentence of this document, signed by Colonel Hasotic, "Our commands and units will continue in full combat readiness to patiently monitor developments and take all measures so that armed conflict does not occur. In this respect, all actions shall be taken in strict compliance with the orders of the superior command." That's what it says, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Mesud Hasotic originally from Sandzak in Serbia wrote at that time, his son was living in Novi Pasar in Serbia, and such a text, he wrote this text to protect his child, among many others, from the -- from the effects of another statement. He also said that he would strictly observe the order of his superior command, which was the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, or rather as of the 20th, the command of the Army of Republika Srpska in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you told the Prosecutor about this document, written by your fellow Bosniak, Colonel Hasotic, is this: "The attitude reflected in this document is why I resigned from the army."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely because of that state of affairs. I anticipated even bigger problems, and with Colonel Hasotic, I disagreed on many points, and we were never friends. We were simply colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what attitude do you see this document reflecting? It talks about things being in bad shape, crime, looting, inter-ethnic reprisals all over the place, predicting difficult times ahead, hoping that conflict can be avoided. I mean, what attitude is that that bothered you? Were you -- how did you object to this attitude? What was your objection?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there were serious problems regarding the personal safety, the safety of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The war in Croatia, which was transferred to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, told me clearly that the army that I had sworn my allegiance did not exist any more and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I therefore could not continue being its member.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, you said this document not being classified, was available to all members of the 5th Corps. Do you know if it was actually distributed to all members of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, no, but I assume, in view of the military chain of command, it must have come down to the level of brigade commands. Whether the brigade commanders then forwarded it to their subordinates, that is something that I do not know. I did not see this document whilst I was an active-duty officer of that army in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go to another subject now. It's correct, isn't it, that prior to 1991, according to your estimate, about 90 per cent of the officers in the JNA were Serb? Immediately prior to 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that 90 per cent were of the Serb and Montenegrin ethnicity, and there is also official information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the -- I know this is easily explainable, but I'm going to have to ask you anyhow, in the Tadic case, your testimony at page 1.211, you were asked this question: "Prior to 1991, to your knowledge, what was the ethnic composition of the officer corps of the JNA?" Your answer, sir, was this: "The data was never officially published but I can say for my unit, and make a rough estimate regarding the situation in the Banja Luka Corps in which I served. In my base, about 90 per cent of the officers were of Serb nationality. The situation was similar at the level of the Banja Luka Corps." That was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what I meant when I said Serb ethnicity, that it was both Serb and Montenegrin, but if that is how it was recorded, that is what I said, but what I meant were Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I said it was easily explainable because I knew you would say that. What I really want to get to is the next one. You then said, "By the end of 1991, that percentage had increased to 99 per cent Serbs." Right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that was because of the war in Croatia and the departure of non-Serb officers from the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I guess it was Wednesday of last week when you started testifying, it's the transcript of the 15 January session, page 12.197, and I don't know if you can remember this particular bit of testimony or not. If not, we'll come back to tomorrow. But you were being asked about the relationship between civilian and military authorities, in 1992, in the area where you were serving, and in answer to one of the questions, you referred to a problem in Teslic between civilian and military authorities. Do you know the problem that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that in Teslic, the mayor of the municipality and his associates were -- did not agree, or rather that there was certain friction between the 5th Corps unit there and the chief of the municipality. And I commented on this because there is also a document about this. There were certain problems because -- and General Talic intervened and said that this problem had to be resolved urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm getting ready to go to a fairly large segment. I think I've got maybe a couple of small issues that I can discuss real quickly from today's testimony and then we can stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of the things I wanted to discuss with you about your testimony today, sir, was you talked about a statement that we heard of General Talic where he used some terms, Turk and Ustasha, which you said were unbecoming an officer and/or anyone who is educated and so forth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I take it you would agree that the same is true of people who would use the term "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except when it comes to paramilitary formations, but I disagree with the term when applied to regular units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And allow me to say that in my military career, I was called a Turk three times. One of those who did that was General Uzelac, General Adzic, and I had serious problems and there was verbal altercation. I am not a Turk, I'm a Bosniak. Turks live in Turkey, not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree with you about that. We saw a segment on the video where Mr. Brdjanin was visiting the front lines, and you were asked what your view was of the reason for his visit to the front lines, and you gave some answer about, well, it was important to -- for recognition of the people that were there fighting and things of that nature. Did you hear what Mr. Brdjanin said about his reason for visiting the front lines?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something I heard, and I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear -- he was asked what his reason was for visiting there and he answered that. Did you hear his answer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot repeat it, but he said he had come to visit units. In a sense, I can't really remember those details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he said that he did that because, I think he said, on Mondays, he was required to report to the presidents of the various crisis staffs in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that makes a great deal of sense, doesn't it? That would have been part of his duties as president of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region, wouldn't it, to report to the presidents of the crisis staffs of the various municipalities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because perhaps the term is a misnomer. He informs and briefs municipal crisis staffs. You report to your superiors, and municipal crisis staffs were at a lower rung but they had to be briefed about what went on in other areas, because municipal crisis staffs did not have the information about what went on, specifically in Kotor Varos, Doboj, or wherever. And that was why the President of the Crisis Staff I toured them and naturally, then, briefed all other municipal crisis staffs, be it in writing or in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So between the two reasons for him going there, his statement as to why he went there and your guess as to why he went there, his statement is probably more accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got the LiveNote in front of me of today's thing but I rather thought my question was not what was the reason for him going there but what was the importance, which is a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm pretty sure although I don't have the LiveNote record that you are right. No, no, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure the word is "reason," and I bet it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're both right, then. We can stop here and take this up tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman. Colonel, we are going to stop here and we can continue tomorrow. Do you think you'll be able to finish tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very unlikely, Your Honour, very unlikely. And I've already told Ms. Korner about that, she knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
